entries.title: How Goalkeeper Sandy MacIver Saved the Spirit’s Season
entries.summary: Filling in for longtime keeper Aubrey Kingsbury, MacIver overcame a shaky start to become a key part of Washington’s success.
entries.content:
Sandy MacIver’s time in the United States didn’t get off to the best start.

Nearly a decade before she became the Washington Spirit’s starting goalkeeper, a young MacIver travelled from her native England to South Carolina to play for Clemson’s women’s soccer team. She had already missed about a month of practices to finish up exams at home and felt unprepared when she arrived late in the summer of 2016.

“It was definitely like, ‘Oh shit, what have I done?’” MacIver told The Sun. “I was in an apartment with three other girls on the team. I [arrive] in the evening from England, and it's like, all right, I don't have any bedsheets, I don’t have anything, I don't have a car to get anywhere. I ended up staying in one of the girl's rooms. … I already felt a bit like a deer in headlights.”

MacIver eventually settled in and started for three years at Clemson before going back to England to begin her professional career at Everton. She had already met Spirit defender Esme Morgan in England’s youth ranks before the duo briefly played together at Everton and Manchester City.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

They reunited again when MacIver joined Washington as a backup at the beginning of last season. With longtime Spirit goalkeeper Aubrey Kingsbury on maternity leave this season, MacIver got her first opportunity in years to be a full-time starter.

MacIver’s previous experience in the U.S., her friendship with Morgan and her first year settling in with the Spirit helped the keeper move past a shaky start and become a crucial piece of Washington’s formidable defense this season. Now, with Washington playing its penultimate regular season game on Sunday, MacIver has franchise-record 11 clean sheets on the year. Last week, she helped the Spirit shut out Gotham FC in a marquee win.

“I hadn't played consistently in maybe even three years, so there's always going to be a bit of an adjustment period,” MacIver said. “It definitely helps playing behind [Tara Rudd] and [Morgan] because they're the people that I'm closest to off the pitch. … Obviously the start of the season wasn't ideal for me, but I got a lot of support from the players and the staff.”

Sandy MacIver Spirit game (4340x2893, AR: 1.50)
After leaving the starting job at Everton in the summer of 2022, MacIver made a handful of appearances for Manchester City and Scotland but struggled to get consistent game time before suffering a rupture to her anterior cruciate ligament while on international duty in April 2024.

After joining Washington in January 2025, MacIver primarily served as a backup to Kingsbury.

The goalkeeper found out she’d be the starter this year when Kingsbury announced her pregnancy at the beginning of the preseason in February. Kingsbury had spent the last eight years as the Spirit’s starter, leaving big shoes to fill.

“Had I known before Christmas, I just wouldn't have been able to enjoy the offseason,” MacIver said. “I'd gone from a point where last season I'm pushing, I'm chasing, I'm just trying to get any opportunity that comes my way. When you know that you're gonna start the season or you're kind of in pole position, the mindset stays the same, but the pressure changes.”
Sandy MacIver AP - 26131059142838 (5163x3442, AR: 1.50)
MacIver conceded four goals in her first three games as full-time starter. But in the fourth match of the year, the goalkeeper kept her first clean sheet in the league in front of an NWSL record 63,004 fans in Denver — the first of four consecutive shutouts for the Spirit.

“There were some difficult moments as a whole team in those first few games, and that's probably difficult for someone coming in and being the No. 1,” Morgan said. “She probably took some blows that she didn't deserve to, but she bounced back.”

MacIver has looked at home in net since, limiting mistakes and producing important saves for a third-place Washington team. Her 11 clean sheets are the most of any goalkeeper in the NWSL, while her 73.7 save percentage ranks third.

“Sandy needed some time, it was her new year playing as a starter … every player needs some time to just adjust and adapt,” coach Adrián González said at a September press conference. “I think she's improving a lot. She's been doing great, and with time, she's had that composure to be able to play, to have great performances.”

MacIver’s four years at Clemson had given her a glimpse of American soccer and its culture, which made adjusting to the NWSL easier. She also benefited from familiar faces like Morgan and midfielder Hal Hershfelt, who was a freshman at Clemson during the goalkeeper’s senior year.

MacIver had the option to join another team in England when she elected to leave Manchester City but went with what she felt would be the better long-term choice in Washington. It also helped that she had visited Morgan in D.C. in 2024 and got to see the area and hear about the defender’s experience with the Spirit.

“Before there was even any chance of me coming to the Spirit, I knew that [Morgan] loved it here,” MacIver said. “She spoke highly of everyone, and so there was no doubt speaking to her that I would like it.”

Sandy MacIver Spirit team (7952x5304, AR: 1.50)Now, MacIver’s apartment is just a few doors down from Morgan’s. They spend time with teammates exploring local restaurants, going to museums or attending concerts (most recently a Pitbull show in August).


“Sandy's one of my closest friends in life, so it's been really nice to have her here,” Morgan said. “We would hang out a lot off the pitch, and because we're both social people, we would often do loads of things with the group, so she didn't need me to help settle. She was kind of the same as I was, just easy to get along with everyone.”


MacIver’s form this season has also translated to international play, where she has starred for Scotland’s national team. The goalkeeper switched her allegiance to Scotland, her father’s country of birth, after representing England as a young player. MacIver has kept five clean sheets in eight games for Scotland this year. Scotland beat Czechia 5-2 on aggregate earlier this month to progress to a two-legged play-off final against Sweden in December, an opportunity for Scotland to qualify for its second World Cup.

“I've loved my time with Scotland,” MacIver said. “How I feel playing for Scotland, if I'd felt like that playing for England, then I would have stayed regardless of selection. But how I feel like walking out onto the pitch, I know I made the right decision.”

Before then, MacIver will aim to continue her strong NWSL campaign with the postseason looming.

“It's just been nice to play football, to be honest,” MacIver said. “The big thing for me is progressing throughout the season and just learning from mistakes. … [I’m] just trying to keep [improving] on the performance before, which for the most part, I've been happy with.”

entries.title: White House Is Weighing Mass Pardons for Junior Staff
entries.summary: Conservative groups influential with the Trump administration have pressed for the preemptive acts of clemency.
entries.content:
White House attorneys are evaluating whether to issue mass pardons to junior staffers, as Trump allies press the administration to protect lower-ranked officials from prosecution and other legal challenges, according to two sources familiar with the conversations.

While President Donald Trump has publicly discussed issuing pardons for top aides and issued pardons for billionaires and major donors, questions have mounted about the potential legal jeopardy facing thousands of employees who have implemented the White House’s agenda.

A pardon for all junior administration personnel is viewed as unlikely, one source said, but the president could issue blanket pardons for all employees involved in particular policy areas, such as deportations, war or trade. Trump has previously said he would be interested in pardoning some administration officials, but the discussions happening now would apply to a far greater number of White House staff than has been previously reported.

Several conservative organizations influential with the administration — including the Heritage Foundation and American Moment — have pressed White House counsel to either prepare pardons or put in place funding for the legal fees necessary to defend junior staffers from criminal and congressional probes or potential lawsuits, according to the two sources familiar with the conversations plus an additional source familiar with the conversations. Mike Davis, a prominent Trump supporter and president of the Article III Project, an advocacy group that fights legal cases for the right, also said he plans to press the White House for action.

These efforts have only intensified, the sources told The Washington Sun, after Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) said earlier this month that congressional investigations into Trump officials should make young Republicans think twice before joining the administration in its final two years.

“After listening to Elissa Slotkin threatening to go after young people who joined the Trump administration, President Trump should issue very broad preemptive pardons for anyone who worked for him or in his orbit,” Davis told The Sun on Friday.

The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

The president has recently shown at least some willingness to penalize potential wrongdoing in his administration. In a rare example of the Trump administration investigating itself, the Justice Department is looking into allegations of contract misconduct against longtime Trump aide Corey Lewandowski.

“All I know is, I want my people to be honest. And if they’re not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted,” Trump told reporters after the Lewandowski news broke.

The White House and The Heritage Foundation did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Nick Solheim, chief executive officer of American Moment, also declined to comment on private conversations. Still, he said: “The president has been very clear he knows the personal, professional and financial risks of Democratic lawfare against people who are affiliated with him and serve him. Political appointees operate on behalf of the president, and I don't have any assumptions other than that the left will do everything in its power to hunt down conservatives who are implementing the president’s agenda.”

Robert Weissman, co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, told The Sun that an impartial Justice Department would look at a range of Trump administration actions that could have broken the law, including unlawful transfers of money between federal agencies, improper use of taxpayer resources for campaigning, contracting arrangements benefiting friends and family of administration officials, and a range of behavior toward immigrants.

Administration officials, Weissman said, “should be worried about being held accountable for violations of civil and criminal law not because future prosecutors may be vindictive but because their jobs would require them to investigate and, if necessary, prosecute the blatant illegalities of the administration.” 

Trump’s Justice Department has also brought legal cases against several of the president’s perceived political foes, including former FBI Director James Comey and two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about their role in the bureau's Hunter Biden investigations.

The planning for potential pardons reflects the accelerating breakdown of long-standing norms over one of the broadest powers granted to the president by the U.S. Constitution. Joe Biden issued more acts of clemency than any prior president and also issued "preemptive pardons" to prominent allies, including several members of his own family, top medical adviser Anthony Fauci and retired Gen. Mark Milley. Trump has taken the pardon power to a new level in his second term, granting clemency to roughly 1,700 people as of June, according to Reuters.

The Justice Department has traditionally housed the formal pardon process, and department officials have vetted candidates before presenting qualified ones to the president. The Trump administration has scrambled that process, though presidents going back decades have also been accused of using pardons to reward friends and allies.

There is likely little a Democratic Congress could do to overturn broad pardons issued by the president. Article 2, Section 2 of the Constitution states that the president "shall have Power to grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offences against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment." The pardon power does not extend to state or local crimes.

Trump has publicly suggested an interest in preemptive pardons for some officials, telling Newsmax earlier this month: “Because these people are lunatics on the, on the left — I don’t want to see people that work for me go through years of nonsense, hire lawyers and everything else, all for nothing.”

Trump has suggested he could pardon himself and has long maintained it is within his right to pardon his officials, citing Biden’s prior actions. The Wall Street Journal reported in April that Trump has also suggested, to “laughs,” pardoning “everyone who has come within 200 feet of the Oval.” Karoline Leavitt, who was then White House press secretary, said at the time: “The Wall Street Journal should learn to take a joke.”

“Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody,” Trump told Time magazine in September. “But you mean I’m not allowed to give them, but Sleepy Joe’s allowed to give them?”

Liz Oyer, the pardon attorney under Biden, said the former president’s pardons set a “really bad precedent” but were limited in scope. Biden did not consult the DOJ’s pardon office before issuing more than a dozen preemptive pardons at the end of his term.

“There have never before been blanket preemptive pardons of everyone in the administration,” Oyer told The Sun. “Preemptive pardons of everyone in the administration, or even of a significant number of administration officials, would be incredibly damaging because they would effectively place the executive branch outside the reach of the law, which would upset the constitutional order of our country in a very fundamental way.”

Widespread pardons for political appointees would be “a new development in American history,” said Mark Osler, a law professor and clemency expert at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.

“It’s a despoilment of what is supposed to be a tool for mercy and national reconciliation being used as a battlefield tool in political wars,” Osler said. “Certainly, the Biden administration did this and blazed the trail, and now it’s potentially being followed in much greater numbers by Trump. I don’t think anyone would conceive that the framers would hope it would be used this way.”
entries.author: Jasmine Wright, Jeff Stein

entries.title: Wizards Struggle on Offense in 112-102 Loss to Raptors
entries.summary: Trae Young had 22 points and 12 assists for the Wizards, who trailed throughout the game. Anthony Davis had just 9 points in his second game for Washington.
entries.content:
Scottie Barnes had 28 points and 14 rebounds, and the Toronto Raptors continued their stellar defensive start to the season with a 112-102 victory over the Washington Wizards on Friday night.

RJ Barrett added 23 points and Kawhi Leonard scored 16 for Toronto, which forced 23 Washington turnovers after Chicago committed 27 in the Raptors’ season-opening victory on Wednesday.

Trae Young had 22 points and 12 assists for the Wizards, who trailed throughout and were down by 17 in the second quarter before closing within a point in the third.

Tre Johnson added 20 points, but Anthony Davis finished with only nine on 3-for-12 shooting in his second career game for Washington. He had 34 points Wednesday in their season-opening victory.

Toronto led 18-6 on the offensive glass and 52-32 in points in the paint.

The Wizards closed within a possession for the first time since the first quarter on Bilal Coulibaly’s layup to make it 64-61 early in the third, and got it to one with a 9-0 run.

Jamison Battle’s 3-pointer made it 81-77 at the end of the third, and Toronto maintained a multiple-possession lead throughout the fourth.

It was all Raptors early.

Barrett and Leonard hit 3-pointers to open the scoring. Collin Murray-Boyles’ steal and dunk stretched it to 22-11 and completed a 12-3 run, and Barrett and Allen Graves hit the first two baskets of the second quarter to make it 38-21.
entries.author: The Associated Press
